tier_reason: The benchmark table in the sdefl.h and sinfl.h header comments compares sdefl 1.0 against zlib 1.2.11, miniz 1.0 and libdeflate 1.3, but gives no CPU, compiler, flags or corpus name, and the repo's only timing code (tests/defl_test.c) times sdefl/sinfl alone with no zlib harness; first-party numbers without methodology are C.

corrections.caveats: First-party table in the sdefl.h/sinfl.h header comments with no CPU, compiler, flags or corpus name; the ratio column implies a 100,000,000-byte input (probably enwik8). The table is laid out like lzbench output, but the comparison harness is not public: the repo's tests/defl_test.c only times sdeflate/sinflate on a file given on the command line (CLOCK_REALTIME, one pass per level) and never calls zlib, miniz or libdeflate. Library versions (sdefl 1.0, zlib 1.2.11, libdeflate 1.3, miniz 1.0) place the run around 2020. The numbers predate correctness fixes merged in March 2025 (PR #56 by lelegard): sinflate()/zsinflate() could overflow the caller's output buffer when it was too small, sdefl_bound() under-reported the worst-case size by 3 bytes (zsdeflate wrote past the reported bound under fuzzing), and decompress-size handling was wrong; the fixes add bounds checks in the decoder, so post-fix speed is unmeasured. The same table shows libdeflate 1.3 clearly ahead of sdefl (147 MB/s compress at -1, 667 to 689 MB/s decompress), so sdefl is faster than zlib but not the fastest deflate. Listed repo vurtun/mmx has been renamed vurtun/lib (the Readme title still says mmx); the comparison picks the sdefl and sinfl components out of a five-header collection (json.h, sched.h, web.h carry zlib/BSD licences). No independent measurements were found (one WebSearch returned nothing on sdefl). Ratios are derived from the page table. Unlicense option carries no patent grant.

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup matches the header table; tier C stands (no methodology, no public comparison harness). Shortcomings to record: no CPU/compiler/flags/corpus, harness not in repo, numbers predate the 2025 decoder buffer-overflow and sdefl_bound fixes (PR #56), libdeflate 1.3 beats it in the same table, last commit 2025-03-19 (stale).

tier_reason: fereidani/musl-vs-glibc publishes benchmark.c and run.sh with the full flag set, names the compiler (zig 0.15.2 using clang 20.1.2) and the CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U), and its README table holds every claimed number, which meets A for a third-party run (same evidence and tier as the catalogued glibc entry, https://github.com/bminor/glibc). The glibc version is not printed (Ubuntu 22.04 host, probably 2.35).

corrections.caveats: Weak, mixed claim: in the musl vs glibc column musl is faster in 9 of 32 rows, slower in 20 and tied in 3; within the record's own category (number parsing/formatting) musl wins atoi_parse (2.3x) and sprintf_float (1.18x) but loses strtod_parse (4.3x slower), sprintf_int (1.21x slower) and snprintf_mix (1.44x slower), all derived from page data. The benchmark is a one-person third-party repo (fereidani/musl-vs-glibc, 7 stars, no licence), one calibrated run per benchmark, one machine, results dated 2025-11-18, glibc version unstated. What was measured is not kraj/musl: it is the musl bundled with zig 0.15.2, built by zig and linked statically, against the host's dynamic glibc through the PLT. Zig 0.15.2 replaces several musl functions with its own code (lib/c/string.zig exports strlen, strcmp, strncmp, strcasecmp; compiler_rt exports memcpy, memmove, memset, memcmp), so those rows do not measure musl. musl's strrchr win depends on the workload and on Zig's strlen: musl implements strrchr as memrchr(s, c, strlen(s)+1), and the 10,000-byte test string has an 'X' every 101 bytes, so the backward scan stops within about 100 bytes while glibc 2.35's forward scan tracks many matches over the whole string. strtok/strtok_r per-token times include a strcpy of the whole input per iteration (glibc's strcpy is faster, so musl's win there is net of that). The memcpy row (glibc 4043.27 vs 154.19 ns for 16 KB) is not a musl result (Zig compiler_rt memcpy) and was tied by the glibc entry's verifier to glibc bug BZ 30994 (rep movsb page aliasing on AMD Zen 3/4; snippet only there, not re-checked here) rather than being a harness artifact. strlen, strcmp and memcmp rows are hoisted no-ops (about 0.1 ns). The earlier statement that -flto=full inlines statically linked musl code is an unverified inference. kraj/musl is Khem Raj's downstream GitHub mirror (default branch kraj/master carries Yocto-style patches; branch master tracks upstream git.musl-libc.org, last commit 2026-10-05); the musl project's own site and git host were not opened (egress blocked). The record is filed under 'musl' because the repo itself carries no benchmark; baseline glibc is not a C++ standard-library facility.

notes: All claimed numbers and the 9/20/3 row count match the README table. Caveats corrected: memcpy row is Zig compiler_rt vs glibc BZ 30994 (not an artifact), Zig 0.15.2 overrides strlen/strcmp/strncmp and mem* so the 'musl' side is partly Zig code, strrchr win is workload-shaped (last match near the end), and in its own category musl loses strtod 4.3x, sprintf_int and snprintf_mix. Kept at A for consistency with the bminor/glibc entry that cites the same benchmark.

tier_reason: ludocode/schemaless-benchmarks publishes the harness (src/mpack/mpack-write.c, mpack-node.c, src/msgpack/msgpack-c-pack.c, msgpack-c-unpack.c, msgpack-cpp-*.cpp, Makefile), the compiler (GCC 5.3.0), flags (-Wall -O3 -flto -fno-fat-lto-objects -DPIC -fPIC -DNDEBUG) and CPU (AMD Phenom II X6 1090T); every claimed number is in its README desktop tables. Author-run, which A allows.

corrections.caveats: Benchmark is written and run by the MPack author (the suite README says it may be biased). Benchmarked versions are MPack 0.8.1 and msgpack-c 1.3.0 (2016 era, GCC 5.3.0 on Arch Linux, Phenom II), while the MPack README now describes MPack 1.1 and msgpack-c 3.3.0 (msgpack-c has since moved to separate C and C++ release lines), so current ratios are unknown. Method: 7 runs of 10 s each, best and worst dropped, a fixed hash time subtracted; output hashes match across the MessagePack encoders, so the work is equivalent. The extended results (full-results-extended.md) add an Intel Celeron 2957U run that agrees: write small 2.19 vs 11.90 us (msgpack C) and 3.44 us (msgpack C++); tree small 8.93 vs 10.34 and 13.15 us. Not all rows are wins: libbson's tree row (4.45 us small, 301.90 us large) is faster, but that row is libbson-iter.c, which walks the BSON buffer in place rather than building a tree, so it is not like for like, and libbson is BSON, not MessagePack. msgpack C's encode row (6.42 us) is the weakest baseline; msgpack C++ is only 1.1x to 1.3x behind on writes. The README claim 'except CWPack' is not backed by the suite, which never benchmarks CWPack (neither README nor full-results-extended.md mentions it). msgpack-c is not in the category's baseline list (iostreams + std::string, std::format). Ratios are derived from the page tables.

notes: All write and tree numbers match the desktop tables of schemaless-benchmarks (small 2367-byte and large 248571-byte MessagePack objects confirmed). Tier A stands; baseline_in_list set to false because msgpack-c is not a listed serialization-json baseline (the CMP entry kept true for the same baseline, so the orchestrator may prefer consistency). Shortcomings: author-run, 2016-era versions and toolchain, libbson faster on its in-place 'tree' row, CWPack claim unbacked by the suite.
